newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North Korean funeral list hints at power struggle.
newsitem.headline: North Korean funeral list hints at power struggle.

text.p: North Korea may be in the throes of a power struggle, analysts and media reports said on Sunday after Pyongyang signalled a major leadership shake-up.
In an apparent bid to show that top leader Kim Jong-il was still in charge, Pyongyang Radio reported his first public appearance since a high-level defection 11 days ago.

Cracks have been appearing in the hierarchy of the secretive communist nation -- already destabilised by food shortages -- since the defection of Hwang Jang-yop, the country's top ideologue, to South Korea's Beijing embassy on February 12.
Premier Kang Song-san, 66, was replaced last Friday. And on Saturday, North Korean media reported the death a day earlier of Defence Minister Choe Kwang, 78.

The line-up of Choe's funeral committee -- a fairly reliable gauge of power -- indicated that the sudden departure of three senior figures was just the latest in a series of exits among the ruling elite.

Large-scale changes since a similar list was issued two years ago has added weight to speculation of a Pyongyang power struggle as Kim prepares at last to assume the formal titles of state president and general secretary of the ruling Worker's Party vacant since his father, Kim Il-sung, died in 1994.

There was no official explanation for the departure of Kang, ranked sixth in the power structure, although he was known to be ailing. Choe, who died of a heart attack, was number seven in the pecking order.
The latest list of 85 names announced by the official North Korean media shows that up to one third of the top 30 positions have changed hands.
"There has been a power shift," South Korea's top newspaper, the Chosun Ilbo, said on Sunday.
"Either they've already been dismissed or there's a serious power struggle inside North Korea," the Dong A Ilbo daily said.
Deputy premiers Choe Yong-rim and Kim Hwan and former premier Yon Hyong-muk were off the list, as was Workers' Party strategy chief O Kuk-ryol and Central Military Commission member Ri Ha-il.
Military men have made the most gains.
"There has been quite a sharp rise in power by military officials," said a report in the Naewoe Press, which monitors the North Korean media.
Japan's Yomiuri Shimbun daily said Workers' Party strategist O enjoyed the support of young military officers and had been believed to be close to Kim Jong-il.
"His disappearance from the funeral list this time around raises the possibility he has been purged or has fallen from grace," the paper said.
The changes "suggest there is a conflict inside Kim's mainstay of support within the country's ruling elite, the so-called 'second revolutionary generation', it said.

"Although Hwang's defection revealed fissures within the Workers' Party, if the struggle for power has spread to the armed forces, which have been the backbone of Kim's new regime, then this casts a long shadow over his future prospects," the daily added.
A broadcast by official Pyongyang Radio, monitored by Tokyo-based Radiopress, reported that Kim Jong-il attended a mass gymnastics display last Thursday.
"The report of Kim's appearance is a signal by North Korea that despite changes he is still in charge," said a Radiopress analyst.
There is speculation Kim Jong-il will formally assume his late father's titles soon, either on the third anniversary of Great Leader Kim's death in July or in the ensuing months.
North Korea is struggling with famine caused by two consecutive years of devastating floods.
To ease its plight, it announced last Friday it would attend a briefing in New York on March 5 on peace talks proposed by the United States and South Korea, which would also include China.

The concession followed promises by Washington and Seoul to send $10 million and $6 million respectively in food aid to the country, which has been at war with South Korea since their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeline Albright, who was visiting South Korea, said on Saturday the success of the talks depended heavily on how economically desperate Pyongyang was.
